clue.text: As per Spooner, secure magnificent property for the King

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words found are said with their beginnings exchanged

parts.note: to lace is to secure or fasten, and grand means magnificent: lace grand

explanation.surface: A buyer trying to obtain a splendid royal estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As per Spooner' exchanges the openings of LACE and GRAND, the way Reverend Spooner muddled his words. 'the King' is Elvis Presley, whose Memphis mansion this is.
explanation.definitionFit: Graceland was the Memphis home of Elvis Presley, known as the King of rock and roll.

clue.text: Mike wearing waistcoat gets drink

indicators.note: a thing being worn sits inside the garment, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a gilet is a sleeveless jacket or waistcoat
Mike is the NATO alphabet word for M

explanation.surface: A man called Mike, dressed in a waistcoat, is handed a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike looks like a person; it is the radio code word for the letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cocktail of gin with lime juice, so it is one kind of alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Like kid in church to be given credit

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons

indicators.note: something in a place is enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
to rib someone is to kid or tease them

explanation.surface: A child in church is somehow rewarded with credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child but is the verb meaning tease. CE, the Church of England, is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit a work to someone is to attribute it to them, which is exactly the verb's meaning.

clue.text: Shy teenage mate uncertain about tense war film

indicators.note: about means around, so the shuffled letters go around another
something uncertain is unsettled, so these letters are not in a fixed order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A bashful adolescent's friend is unsure about a tense war movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads as an adjective describing the film but is the grammatical abbreviation T, placed inside the rearranged phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: This 2001 film depicts sniper duels during the Battle of Stalingrad, so it is a Second World War movie.

clue.text: Clot collecting at the side of cavity

indicators.note: to collect something is to take it in, so one piece is gathered inside another

parts.note: a clot is a fool, as is an ass
by means beside

explanation.surface: A blood clot gathers beside a cavity in the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clot' suggests blood; in Britain it is also mild slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottomless chasm or deep hole is a very large cavity, so the noun fits.

clue.text: Small vessel regularly set sail bearing south at sea to return

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the whole string runs backwards
to bear is to carry, so one piece carries others inside it
regularly means at even intervals, so take every other letter

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
S is the abbreviation for south
taken as written
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A small boat sets out on a southerly bearing and later comes home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' and 'set sail' suggest a ship, but the vessel is a coffee cup. 'Sea' gives the Med, the usual short name for the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a little cup for strong black coffee, and a cup is a vessel for holding liquid.

clue.text: Attempt to grab soft tail of the kangaroo, say

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece holds others inside it

parts.note: a bid is an attempt
P is piano, soft in music

indicators.note: a tail is the very end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone tries to grab hold of a kangaroo's soft tail.
explanation.walkthrough: P for soft comes from musical notation (piano). 'Say' warns that the kangaroo is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A kangaroo moves on its two hind legs, so it is an example of a two-footed animal.

clue.text: Defenders with worries about club meddlers

parts.note: backs are defenders in football or rugby

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: what eats you is what worries you
a driver is a golf club

explanation.surface: A team's defenders are worried about meddling at their club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a sports club; it is a golf club. 'What's eating you?' means what is worrying you.
explanation.definitionFit: These are passengers who give unwanted advice to the driver, so the phrase extends to any interfering busybody.

clue.text: Where one might find bar to see comparatively wacky leader?

definitions.note: a premier is a prime minister or chief, a leader

indicators.note: the clue describes the answer as the word in which bar might be found replacing its opening
the result you would see after the swap is the wacky comparative, so working back exchanges the three letters

parts.note: barmy means wacky, and barmier is its comparative
the word bar itself, taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzle about where to locate a bar to watch an even zanier boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where one might find' bar in the answer, replacing its first three letters, 'to see' BARMIER: so swap BARMIER's BAR back for PRE. There is also a nod to Premier Inn, a British hotel chain with a bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A premier is the chief minister of a government, the person of first rank.

clue.text: Feeling anxious about opening of district festival location

indicators.note: an opening is the start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter
the Reading Festival is a big music festival

explanation.surface: Someone is nervous about the opening of a district's festival site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay. Reading is an English town that hosts a famous annual rock festival.
explanation.definitionFit: To dread something is to fear it in advance, so the participle means worrying ahead of an event.

clue.text: Ridicule male with garden feature — first shed

indicators.note: the first letter of the garden feature is cast off

parts.note: a rockery is a garden bed built of rocks and plants

explanation.surface: Someone laughing at a man whose garden has a shed placed first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shed' looks like the garden building but is the verb: 'first shed' makes ROCKERY lose its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Mockery is derision or taunting, ridicule of someone or something.

clue.text: Son of Scottish ambassador possessing alien weapon

parts.note: Mac in Scottish surnames means son of

indicators.note: to possess is to hold, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: an ambassador is styled His Excellency, HE
ET is the film alien

explanation.surface: A Scottish envoy's son is carrying an extraterrestrial weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: HE, His Excellency, is the formal title of an ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: This broad heavy blade is used for cutting through vegetation and can serve as a weapon.

clue.text: Name of girl vacuously ignoring training

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: vacuously means without content
PT is physical training

explanation.surface: A girl's name is spoken blankly, with no attention to schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: PT, physical training, is removed from the middle of EMPTILY.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common female first name, borne for instance by the novelist Brontë.

clue.text: Met busy first-aiders having no R and R

indicators.note: busy first-aiders bustle about, so their letters are moved around
two letters named next are taken out of the shuffled pool

parts.note: two letters R, the abbreviation standing for rest and recreation

explanation.surface: Overworked paramedics who never get any rest and recreation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having no' takes the two Rs out of FIRSTAIDERS and 'busy' rearranges the remaining nine letters. R and R usually means rest and recreation; here it is just two Rs.
explanation.definitionFit: A need or demand that is met has been fulfilled or answered, i.e. made content.

clue.text: Wasn't distressed?

parts.note: surface reading: stayed calm, did not get upset; setter's reading: dis-tressed, stripped of tresses, so still has a full head of locks

explanation.walkthrough: Split 'distressed' as dis-tressed: tresses are locks, so someone not dis-tressed still has them. The idiom also means stayed calm.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom about keeping hair in place means staying calm, the opposite of getting upset or agitated.

clue.text: Greek character remains imprisoned in centre of Georgian city

parts.note: nu is the thirteenth Greek letter

indicators.note: a prisoner is held inside a cell, so one piece sits within another
the centre is the middle, so only the two central letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of the eight
embers are the remains of a fire

explanation.surface: A Greek man's remains are locked up in the middle of a Georgian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Georgian city' suggests Tbilisi; Georgian only supplies its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a large Bavarian city in Germany, famous for its postwar trials, so it is a city.

clue.text: Reform of Post Office, ditching old computers initially, not on course

indicators.note: reforming something remodels it, so the letters of the two words are rearranged
the letters picked out next are thrown away from the pool
initially means the first letters of old and computers

parts.note: the first letters of old and computers, O and C

explanation.surface: A shake-up of the postal service that scraps its outdated computers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives OC; 'ditching' removes them from POSTOFFICE, and 'Reform of' rearranges the eight letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-piste skiing happens away from the prepared runs, so it is not on a set course.

clue.text: Pampering act with aromatic substance, ceremony scrubbing head

parts.note: a feat is a deed or act
a herb is an aromatic plant used in cooking

indicators.note: scrubbing means wiping out, and head is the opening letter, so the ceremony loses its first letter

parts.note: a wedding is a marriage ceremony

explanation.surface: A spa treatment with fragrant oils given at a ceremony after a head scrub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrubbing head' sounds like hair washing, but it drops the W from WEDDING to leave EDDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Featherbedding means cosseting or spoiling someone, treating them with excessive comfort.

clue.text: Period without working is struggle

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one piece surrounds the others

parts.note: an age is a period of time
a machine that is on is working
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spell without a job is a hard struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but has its old sense of outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To agonise over something is to struggle mentally with it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Not totally claiming to climb plant

indicators.note: in a down answer, climbing means the letters run upwards, so the shortened word is reversed
not totally means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: alleging means claiming or asserting

explanation.surface: Insisting, with some reservations, that a plant can climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not totally' trims ALLEGING to ALLEGIN, and 'to climb' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigella is a genus of flowering plants, including love-in-a-mist.

clue.text: Nuts doubled in such dense food and I might get indigestion

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters are jumbled
the answer together with the named letters might give the long word once mixed

parts.note: the word in written twice

explanation.surface: Someone warning that a heavy meal with nuts piled in will upset their stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer plus IN, IN and I 'might get' INDIGESTION when shuffled, which 'Nuts' signals; 'such' points at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodge is heavy, starchy food that sits in the stomach, the sort that causes indigestion.

clue.text: Place that's unpleasant in sultanate for farmer

parts.note: PL is the address abbreviation for place

indicators.note: something said to be in something else is enclosed by it, so this word signals insertion

parts.note: Oman is a sultanate in Arabia
ugh is the exclamation at something unpleasant

explanation.surface: A farmer finds a disagreeable spot in an Arabian sultanate.
explanation.walkthrough: PL is the street-name abbreviation for Place.
explanation.definitionFit: This worker tills fields with a plough, so he is a traditional farm labourer or farmer.

clue.text: Half-heartedly swindle aristocrat

indicators.note: with half the heart, the doubled middle loses one of its two letters

parts.note: to nobble is to cheat or swindle, in British slang

explanation.surface: Someone half-heartedly tries to con a lord.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart is the middle pair BB; keeping half of it leaves one B.
explanation.definitionFit: A titled member of the aristocracy, such as a duke or earl, is called this as a noun.

clue.text: Casting part in King Otto

indicators.note: a part is a portion, so the letters are a section of the following words

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: An actor is cast in a role as King Otto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casting' and 'part' suggest theatre; casting is a metal block poured in a mould.
explanation.definitionFit: This block of metal is formed by pouring molten metal into a mould, so it is a casting.

clue.text: Runner heading to dispatch one target in alley

parts.note: a ski is a runner, like that of a sledge

indicators.note: dispatching means getting rid of, so one letter is removed from the heading

parts.note: a title is a heading
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An athlete heading off to dispatch a target in a back alley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' looks like an athlete but is SKI; 'heading' gives TITLE, and 'to dispatch' removes I from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A skittle is a pin knocked down by a ball in a skittle or bowling alley.

clue.text: Insect beginning to train showed the way and scuttled

parts.note: a bee is an insect

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter
led means guided, showed the way

explanation.surface: An insect at the front of a line led the way and scurried off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Insect' looks like the definition, which would be the full beetle; here it gives only the shorter insect.
explanation.definitionFit: To beetle off is British for to hurry away with quick short steps, which is to scurry or scamper.

clue.text: Containers of spades moved back in underground tunnel

indicators.note: S, the card abbreviation for spades, is shifted from the front of the word to the end

parts.note: a sewer is an underground drainage tunnel

explanation.surface: Buckets of digging tools hauled back into a tunnel below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: SEWER begins with S, the abbreviation for spades in card games; 'spades moved back' sends it to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewers are large jugs or pitchers, vessels for holding water.

clue.text: Reportedly munch cabbage lacking colour

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so we want the words as they are heard

parts.note: to graze is to munch; kale is a cabbage

explanation.surface: Supposedly someone chews on a pale, colourless cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: Graze kale, said quickly, sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An image in shades of grey only, from black to white, has no hue and so lacks colour.
